label: map_1
name: One-way pykrete flood barges
mech: In winter, shallow moulds on the frozen banks of a river near the mine are flooded with river water mixed with sawdust, and the cold freezes them into thick pykrete hulls. Ore concentrate is sealed inside these hulls in waterproof bags. At spring breakup the hulls float free and ride the flood hundreds of kilometres downstream to an Arctic port or rail point. There the cargo is lifted out and the hull is simply left to melt. A short GPS and ice-thickness log for each hull is used to adjust next year's hull thickness and launch dates to the river's real flood behaviour.
value: Bulk cargo can leave roadless deposits once a year with no steel fleet, no return trips and no road, using a free current and a hull that costs almost nothing.

label: map_1
name: Frost-wedge in-situ ore shattering
mech: In autumn, a dense grid of cheap boreholes is drilled into the ore body and flooded with water. Winter air is then blown or naturally drawn through them, so the water freezes and expands by about 9%. Repeated over several freeze-thaw cycles, this splits the rock along its grain boundaries into fine fragments. Temperature and acoustic sensors in the boreholes record where cracking has slowed, and the next year's water injection is concentrated in those zones. In the thaw season the fines are washed or vacuumed out instead of being blasted and crushed.
value: Most of the cost of blasting, explosives transport and crushing disappears, because the Arctic climate breaks the rock for free.

label: map_1
name: Winter freeze-concentration of leachates
mech: A dilute leach solution or brine carrying metals or rare earths is sprayed or spread in thin layers over a sloped field during winter. Freezing pushes the dissolved salts out of the pure ice, and the concentrated liquid drains away into collecting channels. The spraying rate and the number of passes are adjusted from conductivity readings at the outlet until the target concentration is reached. The ice left behind is nearly clean water that is reused in spring.
value: Concentrating metals before shipping, normally an energy-hungry step, becomes nearly free, so only a small volume of high-grade liquor has to leave the site.

label: map_3
name: Grown pykrete drift barges
mech: In winter, crews repeatedly flood thin layers of river water mixed with wood-chip waste onto riverbank ice. This builds pykrete slabs about 100x30x5 m, each able to float roughly 1,000 t of bagged ore concentrate. The cargo is loaded on top while everything is frozen. At spring breakup the slab floats free, and small tugs steer it down the Lena or Yenisei to an Arctic transshipment port. There it is unloaded and left to melt, so no barge has to go back upstream.
value: Each spring flood becomes a one-way bulk fleet whose only materials are water, sawdust and frost.

label: map_3
name: Cable-hauled ice guideway sleds
mech: Sprinkler rigs build a narrow, graded ice trough along a fixed line from a deposit to a railhead or river. They refresh it automatically whenever the temperature drops enough. Steel-runner ore sleds clip onto an endless steel cable loop, like a ski lift, driven by motors at the two ends. Because runners on ice have friction close to rail, a single loop moves a continuous stream of cargo without trucks, drivers or road surface. Sensors on the track trigger re-spraying wherever the ice wears down.
value: Gives near-railway freight costs every winter for the price of a cable, two winches and a water pump.

label: map_3
name: Permafrost-sealed in-place leaching
mech: Blasting breaks up the ore body underground, and circulating warm brine thaws only a bounded block of it. A leaching solution is then pumped through the block to dissolve the metal, and wells recover it. Any liquid that leaks toward the edge of the block refreezes on contact with the surrounding frozen ground, so the permafrost acts as a self-healing container. Temperature readings at the boundary show where the seal is. Only the recovered metal, often under 1% of the ore's mass, is ever transported.
value: Extracts metals from remote frozen deposits with no pit, no ore haulage and no artificial liner.

label: map_2
name: Disposable Pykrete Flood Barges
mech: In winter, crews cast barge hulls on the frozen river surface near the mine. The hulls are made of pykrete: water frozen with 10-15% local larch sawdust or pulp, which is several times tougher than plain ice. They are filled with ore concentrate or coal and capped with a sprayed ice-and-sawdust lid, insulated with a layer of sawdust. When the ice breaks up in spring, the flood floats them north to an estuary. GPS beacons report their drift, and a few tugs gather them for transfer to sea ships. The hulls are never brought back: they melt into the river, so the transport fleet costs almost nothing to build and needs no return trip. The hull wall thickness and the cargo load are set each year from flood forecasts and from strength tests of the frozen hulls.
value: Any deposit near a north-flowing river can ship bulk cargo once a year with no road, railway or permanent fleet.

label: map_2
name: Autonomous Kite-Sled Freight Trains
mech: Driverless trains of sleds cross frozen tundra and coastal sea ice pulled by large controllable traction kites, like those used to tow ships and on polar expeditions, scaled to tonnes per sled. A small onboard computer steers the kite, picks a route from wind forecasts and ice thickness maps, and anchors the train to wait out calm or unfavourable wind. Each train stores its route log and the ice conditions it meets, and the shared route map improves every season. It has no fuel, road or driver costs, and slow delivery is acceptable for ore stockpiled over the winter.
value: It replaces diesel winter-road trucking with nearly free wind power over the roadless distances where trucking costs the most.

label: map_2
name: Engineered Frost-Shatter Comminution
mech: Broken ore is stacked in insulated heaps laced with pipes and saturated with water. Fans then alternate −40°C winter air with warm water heated by waste heat from stranded gas or a generator. This runs many freeze-thaw cycles per winter instead of one per year. Water expands about 9% when it freezes, which forces cracks open along grain boundaries and shatters the rock to fine sizes. Temperature and acoustic sensors in the heap detect when cracking stops, and the cycle timing is adjusted to match.
value: Most of the crushing and grinding energy, the largest energy cost in hard-rock mining, is replaced by free Arctic cold, so remote deposits can be heap-leached or concentrated on site.

label: g1_genius
name: Transpolar Drift Freight
mech: Sealed, buoyant ore containers with satellite tags are set into Laptev Sea fast ice near the Lena delta. The Transpolar Drift carries the ice and containers to Fram Strait in 2–3 years without fuel or escort. When the floes melt, the containers float in open water and ships pick them up by their tag positions.
value: Bulk ore can reach European waters with no icebreakers, paying only the cost of time.

label: g1_genius
name: Winter-Only Railway
mech: Track panels are laid straight onto snow-compacted frozen tundra, with no permanent embankment, and rivers are crossed on artificially thickened ice. The line runs only during the 5–6 months when the ground is rigid. Each autumn, tamping machines re-level the track to undo the summer heave.
value: Rail-scale bulk capacity reaches remote deposits for a fraction of the cost of an all-season Arctic railway.

label: g1_genius
name: Frozen Placer Dry-Washing
mech: In deep winter, frozen placer gravel is dug and crushed while it stays below −20 °C. At that temperature the ice behaves as a brittle, light mineral. Air tables and dry-washers separate the gold and heavy minerals from gravel and ice by density, with no water at all, and the tailings are stacked frozen.
value: Placer mining can run all year without thawing, water or tailings ponds.

label: g1_mech
name: Buoyant Under-Ice Current Packets
mech: Sealed sacks of about 1 t of ground valuable material each carry a gas bladder, set so the sack is slightly lighter than water and rides pressed against the smooth underside of a frozen river. The current under the ice, which flows all winter, pushes them 25–50 km a day with no fuel or vessel. If a pressure sensor detects a stall, a valve lets out gas so the sack drops back into the flow, then refills it from a cartridge. A net under a slot cut in the ice collects the sacks far downstream.
value: Freight moves along frozen rivers through the whole winter at almost no energy cost, when today nothing moves on them.

label: g1_mech
name: Cold-Dry-Air Charge Sorting
mech: Crushed dry rock is tumbled against a plate so that different minerals pick up different electric charges. The near-zero moisture of −40 °C air stops that charge from leaking away. The grains fall between two charged plates and are pushed into separate bins according to their charge. Readings from each bin continuously adjust the plate voltage and the dividers between bins.
value: Valuable material is separated from waste on site through the winter with no water, cutting the tonnage to be hauled by 5–20 times.

label: g1_mech
name: Stored Meltwater Barge Pulse
mech: In winter, sprayed water builds an ice wall across a small creek, and a peat cover keeps it from melting. Snowmelt fills the basin behind it, and the water is released through a gate in midsummer as a timed crest. Flat-bottomed barges ride the crest down to a river deep enough for ships. Downstream depth gauges control the gate opening so the crest stays deeper than the barges' draft for the whole distance.
value: Creeks that are too shallow for boats become seasonal freight routes from remote deposits, with no road or dredging.
